summary: Year 3 learners mentally add and subtract hundreds to/from a three-digit number with answers below 1000, where only the hundreds digit changes and the tens and ones stay fixed. The core insight is place-value invariance: a known single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) is reused at the scale of hundreds while the other columns are left untouched. Work with a place-value chart, a number line marked in hundreds, base-ten hundred-flats, partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45), and place-value counters on an H-T-O grid; contrast with +tens/+ones (using examples that need no regrouping) so children generalise that an added amount lands in its own column when that column does not go past 9. With answers below 1000 these cases never bridge a thousand.
misconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the hundreds amount to the tens or ones)
Miscounting the hundreds (762 − 400 given as 462 vs correct 362 — a single-digit subtraction slip at the hundreds scale)
Disturbing the tens/ones when they should be untouched
Overreaching to bridge a thousand when the numbers don't require it

activities.title: Freeze the tens and ones: only the hundreds move
steps: Show 345 on a place-value chart (hundreds, tens, ones). Add 200 and watch only the hundreds change from 3 to 5, giving 545 — say aloud that the '45' tail is unchanged.
Now do 762 − 400 on the same chart: the hundreds drop from 7 to 3 while the '62' stays put, giving 362.
Before revealing each answer, point to the tens and ones and state that they will not change, then check after.
Repeat with 518 + 300, predicting the answer (818) and naming which digits stay the same.
Articulate the rule in your own words: the amount you add or take away is a number of hundreds, so it lands only in the hundreds column.
activities.insight: When the answer stays below 1000, adding or subtracting hundreds changes only the hundreds digit; the tens and ones are invariant because the added amount belongs to the hundreds column.

activities.title: Same place-value idea, one column along
steps: Place a +hundreds example (345 + 200) beside a +tens example (345 + 20) and work both.
For each, say which single column changes and read off the two different answers (545 vs 365).
State the shared principle: when the column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), the added amount changes only its own column and leaves the others alone.
Try a mixed set, e.g. 345+200, 345+20, 345+2, naming the changing digit each time before answering.
activities.insight: The place-value rule generalises: whether you add hundreds, tens, or ones, the added amount changes only its own column as long as that column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), as in 345+200, 345+20 and 345+2.

activities.title: Explain what stays the same
steps: After each, answer: which digits changed and which stayed exactly the same, and why?
Answer the probes: How is 762−400 like 7−4, and what is different? If it were 345+20 instead of 345+200, which digit would change?
Explain in a sentence why the tens and ones do not change.
activities.insight: Being able to state that only the hundreds digit changes — and why — demonstrates genuine place-value understanding rather than a memorised procedure.

activities.title: Quick checks for the two common slips
steps: Answer rapid items such as 762 − 400, choosing between 362 and a tempting 462, and justify the correct choice.
Work items that mix +hundreds with +tens (e.g. 345+200 next to 345+20) and state which column moved before answering.
For any item where the tens or ones changed, go back and re-anchor on the chart.
activities.insight: Fast, mixed practice rehearses the skill and exposes wrong-digit and single-digit miscount slips.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 200, then 762 − 400, then 518 + 300. After each, ask which digits changed and which stayed the same.
checkAnswer: 545, 362, 818. In each, only the hundreds digit changes: 3+2=5 hundreds (545); 7−4=3 hundreds (362); 5+3=8 hundreds (818). The tens and ones stay fixed throughout.
